title: Gratitude, again
hook: gratitude of heart, tongue and limbs

segments.voice: Yesterday, patience, and your line: three patiences. Today, the station that walks beside it.

Cracked feet. That's the detail his wife Aisha remembers: the Prophet ﷺ would stand in prayer at night so long that his feet cracked. And she asks the obvious question. Why do this, when Allah has already forgiven you, past and future? If the reason for prayer were fear of punishment, he'd have no reason to stand. His answer, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, turns the whole thing over. Should I not be a grateful servant? He isn't standing to earn something. He's standing to thank someone.
screen: `FEET CRACKED FROM STANDING.` → `WHY, IF YOU'RE FORGIVEN?` → `SHOULD I NOT BE GRATEFUL?`

segments.voice: Gratitude in Arabic is shukr. Al-Ghazali, in the Revival, says it isn't one act but works through the whole person, and he names three places it lives. First, the heart: knowing where the gift came from. Not luck, not only your own effort, but Allah behind the hands that brought it. Second, the tongue: saying it out loud. Alhamdulillah, praise be to Allah, is the plainest form. The Qur'an tells the Prophet, in Pickthall's translation: "Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse." Talk about the good you've been given. Third, the limbs: using a gift the way the giver would love. Eyes used to see kindly. Hands used to help. Strength used to stand at night, as the Prophet did. In the Qur'an, the family of David is told to work in gratitude, so the work itself becomes the thanks. Al-Ghazali needs all three. Thanks in the heart alone stays private. Thanks on the tongue alone can be a reflex, a thank-you said without looking up. Thanks in the limbs alone can become a list of chores. Together it's one motion: I know it's a gift, I say so, and I use it well. And there's a promise, in Pickthall's words: "If ye give thanks, I will give you more." Patience held steady when it's hard. Gratitude is what the same heart does when it's good.
screen: `THE HEART: KNOW WHERE IT CAME FROM.` · `THE TONGUE: SAY IT ALOUD.` · `THE LIMBS: USE IT WELL.` · then, large: `IF YE GIVE THANKS, I WILL GIVE YOU MORE.`

segments.voice: Choose one good thing in your life right now: your hands, a person, the room you're in. First the heart, knowing it's a gift and not something you're owed; then the tongue, a quiet thank you, or alhamdulillah if you pray. Then the limbs: decide one way you'll use that very gift today, hands that help carry something, a voice that calls someone.
Gratitude. Shukr: thanks with the heart that knows the giver, the tongue that says so, and the limbs that use the gift well. Today's word.
Your line: thanks with all of me. Heart, tongue and hands, one motion. Rest well.

howItsDone: Muslims say alhamdulillah, praise be to Allah, throughout the day, after meals, on waking and when asked how they are, and teachers describe gratitude as reaching the heart, the tongue and the deeds of the body.

chat.says: Why would the Prophet pray all night if he was already forgiven?
options: He said, should I not be a grateful servant? He stood to thank, not to earn.
He feared his forgiveness might be taken back if he ever stopped.
He prayed all night only to set a rule that everyone must do the same.
chat.meaning: Aisha asked why he stood so long, and he answered: should I not be a grateful servant? Gratitude, not fear, kept him standing.
